pitch_detail.notes: A bouldery first move off the ground gains a thin finger crack that has some good edges beside it. Protection is thin, the pitch is runout and the climbing feels insecure. An easier low fifth-class line skirts it on the right.
Make an exposed step left, then pick any of several lines of low fifth-class ground up to the ridge crest.

review.changed: Wrote P1 and P2. Left out the 4th-class ridge traverse and the vague third pitch (a choice between continuing along the traverse to the upper bivy site or downclimbing to the top of the slide), which is not a described lead.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches 3 vs 2 true leads plus a ridge traverse; length not checked.

pitch_detail.notes: Begins on the steepest, near-vertical part of the face and eases steadily through less demanding slab to the first chain anchors. Depending on the line chosen, you may reach a second set of anchors instead. Many bolts.
Trend right and up a headwall only about eight feet tall, passing the three-bolt anchor of the neighbouring route Incoming, to finish at the pinnacle of the formation.

review.changed: Wrote two pitches; no grades, lengths or bolt counts are stated per pitch so none were added.

pitch_detail.notes: Thick, vertical pillar in the middle of the flow. It was WI4- on the day it was climbed, so conditions may change the grade. Bring plenty of screws for the fat ice.

A series of WI3 steps separated by lower-angle broken ground, ending in the trees. To descend, use either a pair of 30 m rappels or a single 60 m one. Watch for overhead avalanche danger above the flows; the route gets morning sun.

review.changed: Wrote two pitches. No rappel table: the text gives only rope options (two 30 m or one 60 m), not stations.

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the belay by stepping up, keep mostly to the left side, and run out the pitch to a large chockstone with a partial hourglass shape that makes an excellent anchor; a sling of at least 280 cm is needed to wrap it. The pitch is about 55 m, approximate, and uses nearly a full 60 m rope, so the first belay must sit right at the foot of the chimney or the rope will fall short. Protection is sparse.

Squeeze up the chimney overhead, which offers a couple of enjoyable moves around 5.6 or 5.7. A chockstone caps the chimney: skirt it on the left, take a couple of steps forward, then escape right over loose rock and keep heading directly upward. Continuing straight on is a dead end of dangerously loose, barely attached blocks, and the leader must keep debris away from the belayer. Climbing eases to very low fifth class above the chimney; protection is sparse but the chimney itself takes gear. About 55 m, approximate. The belay is improvised wherever the terrain allows, and choosing the spot is the hard part.

Optional pitch of about 45 m, approximate. Head as straight uphill as possible to a steep outcrop just right of a shallow heather gully, above which the terrain is clearly gentler. The rest of the way to the summit block can be soloed or moved together. The summit block is one pitch of very low fifth class: aim for the notch between its two halves, since heading for the highest point leads onto steep, very loose rock.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P3. Lengths are approximate in the text so kept in notes. No rappel table: the exit is described as rope counts (two single-rope rappels, two double-rope rappels) without anchor detail.

pitch_detail.notes: Step across the seasonal moat and scramble onto the evident ledge at the foot of the route, then climb past two bolts to a single-bolt anchor that doubles as a rappel station.

Climb steep snow early in the season, or a few steps of rock later on, then follow the ledge leftward. A slung block about 30 m along gives an optional belay; replace the webbing if it looks unreliable.

Continue about 30 m further until the ledge terminates at a small alcove. A horizontal crack on its left side, easy to miss unless you bend down, takes the gear anchor: one each of 0.5, 0.75 and 1 in Black Diamond sizing. With a 60 m rope the second and third pitches can be combined into one. Above, either skirt the alcove on its left and scramble to the summit, or escape right just before the alcove. Descend by reversing the route; someone must downclimb this pitch unless gear is left behind.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches. No grades per pitch in the text; none added. No rappel table (descent is the reverse of the route).

pitch_detail.notes: Start from a small ledge at an obvious hand-and-finger splitter and follow it to a wide ledge. Mantle onto it, move right into a yellow corner or chimney, and belay. Rated 5.10+ or 5.11-.
Move left and climb a hanging corner, round an arete, climb a second hanging corner and round another arete to the left, then finish with a hand traverse left to a ledge with a bolted belay.

Face holds lead up and left to a 4 inch crack and a slung flake or horn near large orange roofs. Diagonal cracks then trend up and right to rejoin the main corner. May be easier split into two pitches.
Go up and slightly left through a Yosemite-style V-slot, with finger cracks and stemming sections.
Climb obvious features up and right, passing a small tree, to a belay on a long narrow ledge.
Move the belay rightward, well beyond a large detached flake. The flake can give the impression that the West Ridge or the top of the wall is close; it is not.
Climb up and right on mostly easy ground, with one move around 5.8 about 25 ft above the ledge, aiming for a clean grey V-slot, chimney, gully or groove.
From the upper end of the V-groove, shift right onto a lengthy corner system: roughly 60 m of cracks and corners with a small roof along the way, topping out on finger cracks across a slab.
One brief splitter, thin hands in size, brings easier-angled terrain. Low fifth-class ground then runs on to the summit; alternatively rappel the wall or walk off by the West Ridge or its gully.

review.changed: Wrote all 9 pitches. Grades and lengths only where stated; P1 is a stated range so kept in notes.

pitch_detail.notes: Simul-climb about 65 m of loose ramp trending left, fourth to low fifth class, finishing at five metres of baggy finger crack near 5.6.

About 10 m of blocky ground traversing right leads to a finger crack; the only feet before it come from a small triangular block that slopes outward. Two hard finger moves reach a layback and a mantle, protected with a small cam and a small nut. Move up and right into a hand-and-fist crack with smooth, polished rock, pull a small overhanging move and mantle again, then trend left to another hand crack in a right-facing corner. The gear anchor is on a ledge where a small bush grows.

A hand crack starting at the rear of the belay ledge leads to a small tree. Shift right and work up broken blocky cracks to a bigger tree, which gives a comfortable stance under yet another hand crack.

Good movement off the ground leads to a crack system that narrows with height, then flakes give way to a crimpy rail with slopers and a committing mantle to finish. Protection is poor in places (PG). Three truck-sized flakes are loosely stacked about halfway up; disturbing them could kill the belayer. More precarious flakes sit left of the pitch.
Stem up a corner and an offwidth to a roof split by a thin-hands crack. Gear is good, from ringlocks up to hand sizes. Top out at a slung tree that serves as a rappel station for Green Creek Arete.
Finish on the 5.6 crux section shared with Green Creek Arete.

review.changed: Wrote all 6 pitches with the stated grades and lengths. Rock quality is poor throughout (warned in P4 notes).

pitch_detail.notes: Leave the class 2 gully and head northwest over roughly 50 ft of class 4 rock to a little tree. The final 30 ft up to the notch has low class 5 moves. The notch is a knife-edge above the Crystal Creek ravine, 1,500 ft down, so cresting it feels extremely exposed.

From the notch, make an exposed rightward traverse of about 20 ft beneath an overhanging block, then climb about 25 ft up vertical cracks to a broad cleft separating the two summits. Rope drag will probably call for a quick belay here.
A quick scramble west up about 30 ft of class 4 rock reaches the main summit.

rappel_detail.station: On the summit, down the south face back to the gully.
rappel_detail.notes: One rappel of about 85 ft down the south face returns to the gully.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches; grades only where stated. Lengths are in feet and mixed across sections so kept in notes. Rappel table written for the single south-face rappel.

pitch_detail.notes: Start with easy face climbing up a left-trending rising ledge. Follow the ledge only as far as needed to keep climbing the face; staying on it leads toward the north ridge. Continue on the face to a sandy bench.

Start roughly 10 ft west of the belay, along the bench. A slab with a solid finger crack along its left edge provides pleasant, well-protected climbing and goes straight to the summit, where at least one anchor is in place.

review.changed: Wrote two pitches; no grades or lengths stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb a micro ridge starting about 150 ft right of the route Rampage.
A nice hand crack leads to a ledge.
A shallow corner of about 20 ft off the left side of the ledge, protected only by micro gear dug out of dirt, leads to some sloping ledges. It sits just left of an ugly-looking chimney.
More sloping ledges lead to a nervy, unprotected 5.9 face traverse over gravelly rock, ending at a 4 inch crack.
Follow the wide crack to its top, then continue up the north face of the neighbouring peak for more enjoyable climbing.

review.changed: Wrote five pitches. The notes behind this entry are vague (from an old notebook); no lengths or bolt data given.

pitch_detail.notes: An easy slab brings you to a short, bolted arete that forms the right wall of a left-leaning corner. Keep right of the small stepped roofs; a mantle with some drama then returns you leftward onto the slab higher up.

Simple corners reach an obvious flake. Ascend it about 25 ft, stopping short of a jug shaped like a horn, and cross left with delicate moves on a sloping foot rail. Continue the traverse beneath steep orange rock on closely bolted jugs that bypass loose blocks, and belay at a big, sound block with slings.

Scramble roughly 20 ft over blocks, then step right to layback the conspicuous wide crack. A slab follows; descend a step and go right past the corner to a bolted anchor on a small ledge, arranged so the second can be protected off its upper bolt.

A slabby edge (5.7) gives easy going until it pushes you onto the face. Two well-protected crux moves reach a brief finger-to-hand crack. Beside a big horn, work up and right into another short crack and corner; from its top, step down and left to the wide ledge that sits above the crux pitch of Salad Days. The route merges with Salad Days from here.

review.changed: Wrote P1-P4, the variation start; the text hands over to the upper pitches of Salad Days without describing them here, so pitches 5-9 are not written.

pitch_detail.notes: Direct start. Delicate face moves up the left-trending corner pass a bolt and a fixed pin and cross a small roof into a recess. Work left across friction, then up gentle seams toward a ramp on the skyline. The ramp is highly exposed, and a last stretch of hard friction and face climbing ends at a semi-hanging anchor. Protection: six bolts, one pin and gear to a #1 Camalot.

Step left, then climb up and right on easy grainy rock toward the arete above. Difficulty and rock quality both improve with height. Seven bolts and a few cam placements. The original start instead climbs a 5.8 slab and a 5.9 pitch that ends in loose fourth class below the finger crack, where rockfall has been a concern.
Very sustained thin finger crack with two cruxes, one right off the anchor and the second just before the roof. Gear to 1.75 in.

Climb into a stembox and, before it constricts, exit right to a right-trending crack, ignoring the mid-pitch rappel station. When the crack ends, skip the heathery weakness to the right and instead go directly up past a bolt to a small, blank-looking dihedral. As it ends, stem left to a finger-crack layback. Several mild runouts.
Take the easy corner at the far left, then superb cracks, ending with a steep layback up to an airy belay perch.

Go up a corner for 15 ft. Where suspect blocks begin, exit left past a bolt onto a short slab, then move left again to a finger crack in a right-facing corner. Undercling right around a large roof, then more cracks lead to an anchor at the base of the final slabs.
Easy slabs and overlaps lead to the ridge crest. Beware of loose rock. Links with the previous pitch.
Move the belay across exposed third class to the base of the summit block, taking 1 to 2 in cams. A difficult mantle gives way to easier climbing and a summit; only three draws are needed.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches using the direct start for P1-P2 (the original start is noted in P2). Feet converted to metres. No rappel table: descent is described as ten rappels with a 70 m rope but the stations are not individually listed.

pitch_detail.notes: Delicate face moves up the left-trending corner cross a small roof into a recess. Work left across friction, then up gentle seams toward a ramp on the skyline. The ramp is airy, and a last stretch of hard friction and face climbing ends at a semi-hanging anchor. Six bolts and one pin, plus gear to a #1 Camalot. Long slings help with rope drag. A true 70 m rope can rappel this pitch but it is free-hanging and barely reaches the ledge; extend the rappel if unsure and send the first person down on a single strand.

Move left, then angle up and right across easy, grainy rock toward the arete overhead. Both difficulty and rock quality rise as you gain height. Seven bolts and a few cam placements. About 40 ft of solid third-class ground then leads to the start of the next pitch.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. No rappel table: only a note about rappelling the first pitch with a 70 m rope.
